Chapter 11: Administering Azure Networking

Exploring Azure Networking Services
Azure offers a wide range of networking services for its users. Following are some of the key networking services offered by Azure:
Virtual Network (VNet)
Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is a logical isolation of Azure cloud services that provides a secure and private network environment in the cloud. With VNets, users can connect to Azure resources such as VMs, load balancers, and other Azure services using private IP addresses. Users can also create subnets within the VNet to segment resources and apply network security controls such as Network Security Groups (NSGs).
VPN Gateway
Azure VPN Gateway provides a secure connection between on-premises networks and Azure VNets over the public Internet. Users can connect to Azure using site-to-site or point-to-site VPN connections. Site-to-site VPN connections allow users to connect their on-premises network to an Azure VNet, while point-to-site VPN connections allow users to connect individual devices to Azure over the Internet.
ExpressRoute
ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection between on-premises infrastructure and Azure. This connection is provided through a connectivity provider, such as an Internet Service Provider (ISP), and is more reliable, predictable, and faster than a VPN connection over the public Internet. ExpressRoute also provides a more secure connection by bypassing the Internet.
Load Balancer
Azure Load Balancer provides high availability and scalability for virtual machines and applications. It distributes incoming traffic across multiple VMs and can be used for both internal and external load balancing.
Application Gateway
Azure Application Gateway is a web traffic load balancer that provides advanced routing and SSL termination capabilities for web applications. It can also provide additional security features such as Web Application Firewall (WAF).
Azure Firewall
Azure Firewall is a managed, cloud-based network security service that provides firewall capabilities for VNets. It is a fully stateful firewall that can be centrally managed and provides high availability and scalability.
Network Security Groups (NSGs)
Azure NSGs are a cloud-based firewall that allows users to filter network traffic to and from Azure resources. NSGs can be applied to subnets or individual VMs, and they can be used to filter traffic based on IP addresses, ports, and protocols.
Azure Bastion
Azure Bastion provides secure and seamless RDP/SSH connectivity to Azure VMs using a browser-based interface. It eliminates the need for a public IP address or VPN connection to access Azure VMs.
Azure DNS
Azure DNS is a fully managed DNS service that provides high availability and scalability for domain name resolution. Users can create and manage DNS zones and records within Azure, and integrate Azure DNS with their on-premises DNS infrastructure.
Traffic Manager
Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based traffic load balancer that can be used to distribute incoming traffic across multiple endpoints, including Azure VMs, cloud services, and external endpoints. It provides automatic failover capabilities and can be used to optimize global application performance.
Overall, Azure offers a comprehensive set of networking services that allow users to build secure, scalable, and highly available network architectures in the cloud. These services include VNets, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Azure Firewall, NSGs, Azure Bastion, Azure DNS, and Traffic Manager.

Popularity of Azure Bastion
Azure Bastion is a fully-managed Platform as a Service (PaaS) solution provided by Microsoft Azure. It allows secure and seamless Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and Secure Shell (SSH) connectivity to Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) over the Internet using a web-based gateway.
Azure Bastion is used to provide a secure, and easy-to-use remote access solution to VMs in Azure, without exposing the VMs directly to the Internet or requiring a virtual private network (VPN) connection. It helps to simplify the management of remote connectivity, as there is no need to configure public IP addresses, network security groups (NSGs), or VPN gateways.
With Azure Bastion, users can connect to a VM using just a web browser and access the remote desktop or command-line interface, eliminating the need for additional tools or clients. The traffic between the client and Azure Bastion is encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS), providing an extra layer of security.
Azure Bastion is particularly useful for scenarios where users need to access VMs in a secure manner, such as managing applications or configuring infrastructure, from anywhere with an internet connection. It is also helpful in cases where corporate policies restrict the use of VPN or require multi-factor authentication for remote access.

Setting Up Remote Desktop Protocol
Create VNet with Azure CLI
First, we need to create a Virtual Network (VNet) with a subnet that will host the bastion resource. We can do this using the Azure Portal or Azure CLI. Following is an example using the Azure CLI:
az network vnet create \
   --resource-group myResourceGroup \
   --name myVnet \
   --address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/16 \
   --subnet-name mySubnet \
   --subnet-prefixes 10.0.0.0/24
Create Public IP
Next, we need to create a public IP address that will be used by the bastion resource:
az network public-ip create \
   --resource-group myResourceGroup \
   --name myPublicIp \
   --sku Standard \
   --allocation-method Static
Now, we can create the bastion resource itself:
lua
Copy code
az network bastion create \
   --resource-group myResourceGroup \
   --name myBastion \
   --vnet-name myVnet \
   --location eastus \
   --public-ip-address myPublicIp
This will create a new bastion resource named "myBastion" in the "eastus" region, using the "myVnet" VNet and "myPublicIp" public IP address.
Once the bastion is created, we can use it to securely connect to a virtual machine in the same VNet. To do this, we can use the Azure Portal or Azure CLI to configure the virtual machine's network settings to allow connections from the bastion resource.
Connect to VM using Azure CLI
Following is an example using the Azure CLI:
az vm access allow \
   --resource-group myResourceGroup \
   --name myVM \
   --port 3389 \
   --protocol tcp \
   --from-bastion
This command will allow RDP (TCP port 3389) connections from the bastion resource to the "myVM" virtual machine.
Finally, we can connect to the virtual machine using the Azure Portal or Azure CLI.
Connect to VM using Azure Portal
Following is an example using the Azure Portal:
●       Navigate to the "myBastion" bastion resource in the Azure Portal.
●       Click "Connect".
●       Select the virtual machine ("myVM") from the list.
●       Enter your username and password.
●       Click "Connect".
This will launch an RDP session to the virtual machine via the bastion resource.

Setting Up VPN Gateway
Step-By-Step Procedure to Establish VPN
To set up a VPN gateway in Azure, follow these steps:
Sign in to the Azure portal and navigate to the Virtual Network gateway you want to create.
Click on the "+ Add" button to create a new gateway.
Select "VPN" as the gateway type and choose the VPN routing type that best suits your needs. Click "Next: IP configuration".
On the IP configuration page, select "Dynamic routing" as the gateway SKU and configure the IP address settings for your gateway subnet.
Create or select an existing public IP address to use for the VPN gateway, and then configure the rest of the settings for your gateway.
Click "Review + create" to review your settings and then click "Create" to create the VPN gateway.
Once the gateway is created, configure your on-premises VPN device to connect to the gateway using the IP address and shared key provided in the Azure portal.
Once the connection is established, you can test the connection to ensure it's working properly.
Creating VPN using Azure CLI
Following is a sample code in Azure CLI to create a VPN gateway:
# Create a resource group
az group create --name MyResourceGroup --location eastus
# Create a virtual network
az network vnet create --resource-group MyResourceGroup --name MyVNet --address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/16 --subnet-name MySubnet --subnet-prefix 10.0.0.0/24
# Create a public IP address for the VPN gateway
az network public-ip create --resource-group MyResourceGroup --name MyGatewayIP --allocation-method Dynamic
# Create a VPN gateway
az network vnet-gateway create --resource-group MyResourceGroup --name MyGateway --public-ip-address MyGatewayIP --vnet MyVNet --gateway-type Vpn --vpn-type RouteBased --sku VpnGw1 --no-wait
This code will create a VPN gateway named "MyGateway" in a virtual network named "MyVNet" with a subnet named "MySubnet". The VPN gateway will use a public IP address named "MyGatewayIP" with a dynamic allocation method.

Configure Load Balancers
Azure Load Balancer is a Layer-4 load balancer that provides high availability by distributing incoming traffic among healthy instances of services. It offers two types of load balancing - inbound and outbound. Inbound load balancing distributes incoming traffic to backend pool instances, while outbound load balancing distributes outbound traffic from instances to external endpoints.
Stages to Configure Azure Load Balancers
To configure an Azure Load Balancer, you can follow these steps:
Create a backend pool
A backend pool is a group of virtual machines that will receive traffic from the load balancer. You can create a backend pool by specifying the IP addresses of the virtual machines or by selecting a virtual machine scale set.
Create a health probe
A health probe checks the health of the backend pool instances and marks them as healthy or unhealthy based on their responses. You can create a health probe by specifying the protocol, port, and path to test.
Create a load balancing rule
A load balancing rule maps a frontend IP address and port to a backend pool. You can create a load balancing rule by specifying the frontend IP address and port, the backend pool, and the health probe.
Managing Load Balancers
Once you have created the Azure Load Balancer, you can manage it in several ways:
●        Scaling: You can scale the Azure Load Balancer horizontally by adding more backend pool instances or vertically by upgrading the load balancer to a higher SKU.
●        Monitoring: Azure Load Balancer integrates with Azure Monitor to provide metrics and logs for monitoring the load balancer and its backend pool instances.
●        Traffic distribution: You can control how the Azure Load Balancer distributes traffic to the backend pool instances by configuring load balancing algorithms and session persistence.
●        SSL offloading: Azure Load Balancer supports SSL offloading, which enables the load balancer to terminate SSL/TLS connections and forward decrypted traffic to the backend pool instances.
●        Availability zones: Azure Load Balancer supports deployment in availability zones, which provides additional fault tolerance and high availability.
Create Load Balancers using Azure Portal
Following is an example of how to create an Azure Load Balancer using the Azure portal:
Go to the Azure portal and select "Create a resource".
Search for "Load Balancer" and select "Load Balancer".
Select the subscription, resource group, and name for the load balancer.
Select the type of load balancer - Standard or Basic.
Configure the frontend IP address and port.
Configure the backend pool and health probe.
Configure the load balancing rule.
Review and create the load balancer.
Once the load balancer is created, you can manage it from the Azure portal or using the Azure CLI or PowerShell.

Azure Network Watcher for Network Issues
Following is a sample program showing how to use Azure Network Watcher to monitor and diagnose network issues:
First, navigate to the Azure portal and search for "Network Watcher" in the search bar.
Click on "Network Watcher" and then select the region where your virtual network is located.
In the Network Watcher dashboard, you will see several tools that can be used to monitor and diagnose network issues. For example, the "Topology" tool can be used to visualize the connections between virtual machines and subnets in your virtual network.
To use the "Connection Monitor" tool, navigate to the "Connection Monitor" tab and click on "Add" to create a new connection monitor.
Follow the wizard to specify the source and destination of the connection monitor, as well as the protocol and port that should be monitored.
Once the connection monitor is created, you can view the status of the connection and any alerts that are generated by navigating to the "Connection Monitor" tab.
You can also use the "Packet Capture" tool to capture and analyze network traffic in your virtual network. To use this tool, navigate to the "Packet Capture" tab and click on "New capture" to create a new capture.
Follow the wizard to specify the source and destination of the capture, as well as any filters that should be applied.
Once the capture is started, you can download the capture file and analyze it using a tool such as Wireshark.
Finally, the "IP Flow Verify" tool can be used to verify that traffic is flowing correctly between two virtual machines in your virtual network. To use this tool, navigate to the "IP Flow Verify" tab and follow the wizard to specify the source and destination of the traffic.
Overall, with Azure Network Watcher, you can monitor and diagnose network issues in your virtual network, allowing you to quickly troubleshoot and resolve any issues that arise.
